name: Italian Game
description: A classical opening focusing on rapid development and central control.

intro: The Italian Game is one of the oldest openings in chess — players have used it for over 500 years.
Its core idea is simple: develop pieces quickly, control the center, and aim at f7 — Black's weakest square.

messages: 1. e4 — the King's Pawn opens our game.
This stakes a claim in the center and frees both the bishop and the queen.
1...e5 — Black mirrors, contesting the center directly.
2. Nf3 — we develop a knight and attack the e5 pawn at the same time.
Notice how each move accomplishes multiple goals: development plus pressure.
2...Nc6 — Black defends e5 with a natural developing move.
3. Bc4 — the Italian bishop takes aim.
This bishop points right at f7, the only square defended solely by Black's king.

outro: We've reached the starting position of the Italian Game.
From here, Black has several solid replies — the Giuoco Piano, the Two Knights, or the Hungarian Defense.
Pick a variation to see how Black responds and how the game develops.

variations.name: Giuoco Piano
variations.description: The quiet game - a solid positional approach to the Italian Game.

intro: The Giuoco Piano — Italian for 'quiet game' — is the classical answer to the Italian.
Black mirrors White's setup, leading to slow, positional play.

messages: 1. e4 stakes our claim in the center.
2. Nf3 develops with tempo, attacking e5.
3. Bc4 — the Italian bishop, eyeing f7.
3...Bc5 — Black mirrors with the bishop, also targeting f2.
Both sides have symmetrical pressure on the weakest squares — the 'quiet game' is set.

outro: The Giuoco Piano is famous for slow, manoeuvring play.
White typically plays c3 and d3 to support a later d4 break.
Despite its quiet name, both sides have rich strategic and tactical possibilities.

variations.name: Two Knights Defense
variations.description: Sharp tactical play with early knight development.

intro: The Two Knights Defense is the sharp, aggressive reply to the Italian Game.
Black ignores the bishop on c4 and develops a second knight with a threat of its own.

messages: 3. Bc4 — the Italian bishop is in place.
3...Nf6 — Black develops the second knight and attacks White's e4 pawn.
This signals an intent to fight: tactics are coming.

outro: The Two Knights leads to some of the sharpest play in classical openings.
White's most ambitious choice now is 4. Ng5, attacking f7 directly.
Be ready for tactics — this variation has trapped many players over the centuries.

variations.name: Hungarian Defense
variations.description: A solid but passive defense for Black.

intro: The Hungarian Defense is the solid but modest reply to the Italian Game.
Black avoids tactical complications and aims for a safe, passive setup.

messages: 3...Be7 — Black quietly tucks the bishop away.
This avoids the sharper Giuoco Piano and the tactical Two Knights, at the cost of activity.

outro: The Hungarian Defense is rare at the top level — Black gives up activity for safety.
White typically gets a small but stable edge with patient play.
Useful to know defensively, even if you rarely play it.

name: Queen's Gambit
description: A strategic opening offering a pawn to gain central control.

intro: The Queen's Gambit is one of the most respected openings at every level — from beginner to world champion.
It's not really a gambit: White offers the c-pawn but can usually win it back. The real goal is to undermine Black's center.

messages: Solid, strategic, and a favorite of positional players.
1...d5 — Black contests the center directly, just as e5 does against e4.
It pressures d5 and offers the c-pawn. If Black takes, White's d4 will dominate the center.

outro: Black now chooses how to handle the offer.
Take the pawn (Accepted), defend with e6 (Declined), or support d5 with c6 (Slav).
Each leads to a completely different middlegame.

intro: The Queen's Gambit Accepted: Black grabs the pawn and trusts White will struggle to win it back.
Modern theory says White does get the pawn back, but Black gains time to develop.

messages: 2. c4 — the gambit pawn is offered.
Black temporarily wins a pawn but cedes the center. White will play e3 or Nf3 and recapture the pawn later.

outro: The Accepted leads to open positions with active piece play.
Black aims for quick development with c5 to undermine d4 once the c-pawn is recovered.

variations.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
variations.description: Black declines the gambit and maintains central tension.

intro: The Queen's Gambit Declined is one of the most solid responses Black can choose.
Black supports d5 with the e-pawn and prepares calm piece development.

messages: 2...e6 — Black declines, supporting d5 with the pawn.
The trade-off: the c8-bishop is now blocked behind its own pawn. Freeing it will be a project.

outro: The QGD leads to slow, manoeuvring positions where both sides build up patiently.
World champions like Karpov and Anand built careers on this rock-solid setup.

variations.name: Slav Defense
variations.description: A solid defense supporting the d5 pawn with c6.

intro: The Slav Defense supports d5 with the c-pawn instead of the e-pawn — keeping the c8-bishop's diagonal open.
It's considered one of the most reliable defenses in chess.

messages: 2...c6 — the Slav. Black supports d5 without locking in the bishop.
If Black later plays e6, it's a Semi-Slav — combining the best of both worlds.

outro: The Slav is famous for resilience and is favored by players who like clear plans.
Key idea: develop the c8-bishop to f5 or g4 before playing e6.

name: Sicilian Defense
description: Black's most popular response to e4, leading to sharp tactical play.

intro: The Sicilian Defense is the most popular response to 1. e4 above club level.
Black refuses symmetry and immediately fights for an unbalanced position.

messages: Instead of mirroring with e5, Black challenges d4 from the side and aims for sharp, asymmetric play.

outro: Black accepts a slightly cramped position in exchange for long-term winning chances.
From here, the game branches into hundreds of named variations — Najdorf, Dragon, Sveshnikov, Taimanov, and more.
Pick a variation to see one popular continuation.

variations.name: Sicilian Najdorf
variations.description: The most popular and sharp variation of the Sicilian.

intro: The Najdorf is the most famous Sicilian variation — Bobby Fischer's lifelong weapon.
It's flexible, deeply theoretical, and demands precise play from both sides.

messages: 2...d6 — Black prepares Nf6 without allowing e5.
4. Nxd4 — White's knight reaches a strong central square.
This little pawn move prevents Nb5 and prepares ...b5 to expand on the queenside.

outro: The Najdorf creates one of the most studied positions in chess.
White has many options here — 6. Be3 (English Attack), 6. Bg5 (sharpest), 6. Be2 (positional), and more.
Don't memorize raw lines — understand the typical plans for both sides.

variations.name: Sicilian Dragon
variations.description: A hypermodern setup with fianchettoed bishop.

intro: The Sicilian Dragon — Black's setup with the bishop on g7 looks like a fire-breathing dragon along the long diagonal.
Both sides usually attack opposite kings. Pure violence.

messages: Black will play Bg7, putting the bishop on the long diagonal aiming at White's queenside.

outro: The Dragon leads to opposite-side castling and races to mate.
White's main weapon is the Yugoslav Attack: Be3, Qd2, O-O-O, then h4–h5 to pry open the kingside.
Memorize key tactics — one slow move can lose the game.

variations.name: Sicilian Accelerated Dragon
variations.description: An early g6 setup avoiding some of White's attacking lines.

intro: The Accelerated Dragon plays the fianchetto without ...d6, hoping to avoid the Yugoslav Attack.
The trade-off: White can play c4 with strong central control — the Maroczy Bind.

messages: Black commits to the dragon setup quickly, without first playing d6.
4...Bg7 — the dragon bishop reaches its diagonal.
Black aims for fast development and pressure on the long diagonal.

outro: If White plays c4 here, you get the Maroczy Bind — a tough position to crack.
Black plays for piece activity and a timely d5 break to free the position.

name: French Defense
description: A solid defense creating a strong pawn chain.

intro: The French Defense is a classical response to 1. e4 that favors solidity over symmetry.
Black plans ...d5 to challenge White's e4 pawn from the side.

messages: Black prepares d5 without committing the c8-bishop's exit yet. The cost: that bishop will often be locked in.

outro: From here, White typically plays 2. d4 d5 and the game branches: Advance (3. e5), Exchange (3. exd5), Tarrasch (3. Nd2), or Classical (3. Nc3).
The French is a great choice if you like solid, strategic positions.

variations.name: French Winawer
variations.description: Sharp tactical play with early bishop pin.

intro: The French Winawer is one of the sharpest and most complex French variations.
Black pins the c3 knight and is willing to accept doubled pawns to wreck White's structure.

messages: Black threatens to capture on c3 and double White's pawns. If White wants to keep pawns intact, the knight must move or be defended.

outro: Mainline: 4. e5 c5 5. a3 Bxc3+ 6. bxc3 — White accepts doubled c-pawns for the bishop pair.
Both sides have long-term structural goals; this is positional chess at its richest.

variations.name: French Classical
variations.description: Classical development with knight to f6.

intro: The French Classical develops the knight to f6 and attacks the e4 pawn directly.
White must decide: advance the pawn, exchange, or defend it.

messages: Black puts immediate pressure on e4 with a natural piece move.

outro: White usually plays 4. e5, kicking the knight and gaining space. The position becomes a battle for the e5 outpost.
Black aims for ...c5 to challenge d4 and free the cramped position.

name: Ruy Lopez
description: One of the oldest chess openings, named after a Spanish priest.

intro: The Ruy Lopez — also called the Spanish Game — is one of the oldest and most respected openings.
White's bishop pins the c6 knight against the king, putting long-term pressure on Black's center.

messages: It pins the c6 knight and threatens to disrupt Black's center. This is the move that launched a thousand games.

outro: From here, Black has two main paths: 3...a6 (the Morphy Defense, mainline) or 3...Nf6 (the Berlin Defense, super-solid).
Each leads to entirely different middlegames.

variations.name: Ruy Lopez Berlin
variations.description: The Berlin Defense - a solid equalizing system.

intro: The Berlin Defense became famous when Vladimir Kramnik used it to beat Garry Kasparov for the world title.
Black develops calmly and is happy to enter the Berlin Endgame — a position once thought lifeless, now considered rock solid.

messages: Black ignores the bishop's pin and attacks e4. If White plays 4. O-O, Black can grab the pawn with Nxe4.

outro: Mainline: 4. O-O Nxe4 5. d4 — leading to the Berlin Endgame after a queen trade.
It's a high-level drawing weapon and a great way to neutralize an aggressive opponent.

variations.name: Ruy Lopez Morphy
variations.description: The main line with a6 attacking the bishop.

intro: The Morphy Defense is the most popular reply to the Ruy Lopez at every level.
Black's tiny pawn move 3...a6 asks the bishop a question — and shapes the entire game.

messages: Black asks the bishop: do you retreat, or capture? If 4. Bxc6 dxc6 Black gets the bishop pair; if 4. Ba4, the typical Closed Ruy Lopez begins.

outro: After 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O, the game enters the heart of Ruy Lopez theory.
It's a vast and rich opening — entire careers have been built studying just this position.

name: King's Indian Defense
description: A hypermodern defense allowing White central control initially.

intro: The King's Indian Defense is one of Black's most aggressive openings — favored by Fischer, Kasparov, and Nakamura.
Black willingly cedes the center early, planning to attack it later with pieces and pawn breaks.

messages: 1...Nf6 — Black develops the knight and prevents 2. e4.
2. c4 — White claims more central space.
Black prepares to fianchetto the bishop on g7, where it will aim straight across the long diagonal.

outro: The King's Indian is a hypermodern opening: let White build a big center, then strike at it.
Common plans involve ...e5 and ...f5, launching a kingside attack while White attacks on the queenside.
It's a fighter's opening — draws are rare.

name: English Opening
description: A flexible opening controlling the center from the flank.

intro: The English Opening is a flexible, hypermodern way to start the game.
White controls the center indirectly with c4 and can transpose into many other systems.

messages: Instead of grabbing the center with a pawn, White attacks d5 from the side and keeps options open.

outro: The English can transpose into the Queen's Gambit, Réti, or stay independent.
It's a favorite of players who like to control the game's character before their opponent can dictate it.
Common follow-ups: 1...c5 (Symmetrical), 1...e5 (Reversed Sicilian), 1...Nf6 (flexible).

name: Caro-Kann Defense
description: A solid defense similar to the French but more flexible.

intro: The Caro-Kann is the solid alternative to the Sicilian and the French.
Black prepares ...d5 with the c-pawn — supporting it without blocking the c8-bishop like in the French.

messages: 1. e4 — White's most popular first move.
Black quietly prepares 2...d5, planning to develop the c8-bishop actively, unlike in the French.

outro: The Caro-Kann is a favorite for players who want to avoid memorization wars.
Mainline: 2. d4 d5 3. Nc3 dxe4 4. Nxe4, with Black playing for solid development and a small structural edge.
It's been called 'the underground railroad to a draw' — but at high level it's far more than that.
